newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right's last hope - a Seguin-Madelin ticket?.
newsitem.headline: French right's last hope - a Seguin-Madelin ticket?.

text.p: France's centre-right coalition unveiled its last card on Wednesday in an increasingly desperate election campaign -- an odd tandem of socially-minded Gaullist Philippe Seguin and militant free-marketeer Alain Madelin.
Political commentators described the unlikely duo, who embody radically different approaches to economic and social policy, as "the marriage of the carp and the rabbit".
It may be a brief marriage, with the odds now on a leftist alliance completing a stunning upset by winning next Sunday's parliamentary election runoff.
Seguin and Madelin were to share a platform at a rally in the Alpine city of Chambery on Wednesday night.
President Jacques Chirac has left the electorate guessing whom he might choose to replace outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe if the right managed to salvage Sunday's decisive second round vote.

Political sources said that if the right won, the likely scenario was that Seguin would be appointed prime minister and Madelin finance minister, although Chirac gave no hint of that in a television address on Tuesday night.

The two have little in common on policy, but both supported Chirac's presidential campaign and both have been out of power since Madelin was fired as finance minister in August 1995 for attacking civil servants' "privileges".

Seguin, 54, spearheaded the campaign for a "no" to the Maastricht treaty on European economic and monetary union in a 1992 French referendum and remains deeply critical of what he calls the "ultraliberal drift" of the European Union.
Professing to believe in a "tempered liberalism", he stresses the central role of a strong, protective state.
Madelin, 51, is France's nearest thing to a Thatcherite. He advocates shrinking the state, cutting taxes and freeing up private initiative.
But in a radio interview on Wednesday, he insisted his views were not incompatible with Seguin's.

Asked whether Chirac had given his blessing to a Seguin-Madelin electoral "ticket", Madelin said: "The president knows that we are holding rallies together and I think he would not object. People sometimes try to put us in opposition to each other, but you have to look at what joins us together."

Asked what he and Seguin had in common, he said: "There is one common point, which is the feeling that we have to govern for the people, that many of the public's hopes are orphaned today and that we cannot confine the power to the corridors of the senior civil service."
Seguin has sought to take a more orthodox line on European monetary union as the prospect of replacing Juppe has grown, saying France's signature on the Maastricht treaty must be respected.

But in an intervew with this week's L'Express magazine, he rejected an over-strict interpretation of the criteria for monetary union, calling the deficit limit of three percent of gross domestic product "masochistic" in a period of slow growth.

Seguin also said that once the German public had been persuaded to accept a single currency, he hoped the financial "straitjacket" on European governments could be loosened to put employment at the centre of the EU's policy.
Madelin has sought to smooth the sharper edges of his rhetoric during the campaign, stressing that he wants to preserve a renovated version of France's welfare state.

But the self-made intellectual drew widespread criticism after one campaign outburst against France's elite Ecole Nationale d'Administration civil service college, which he implicitly compared to a criminal or terrorist organisation.
"The English have the IRA, the Spanish have ETA, the Italians have the Mafia and we have ENA," Madelin said.
Ironically, Seguin is a graduate of ENA.
